title: How Does the Hawthorne Effect Influence Teachers' Wait Times?
author: Busch, Bradley
summary: Bradley Busch applies the Hawthorne Effect, the 1924 finding that workers change behaviour simply because they know they're being observed, to what happens to teachers' wait times specifically during lesson observations. He argues observed teachers often unconsciously shorten wait time due to "action bias," the discomfort of silence pushing them to fill it with more talk or a follow-up question rather than letting students genuinely process. He then connects shortened wait time to concrete downstream harms for students: reduced cognitive processing time, decreased participation, particularly from students who need longer to formulate a response or feel less confident, and increased classroom stress and anxiety from an artificially rapid pace. His three countermeasures are practical rather than aspirational: silently counting wait time to guard against unconsciously rushing, deliberately keeping the classroom routine as close to normal as possible during an observation to reduce the anxiety that drives action bias, and self-reflecting on personal wait-time habits outside the pressure of being watched, to build a baseline the teacher can trust.
points: Busch's key mechanism is naming action bias as the specific psychological driver connecting "being observed" to "shorter wait times," rather than treating the link as simple nervousness.
His downstream-harms framing, reduced processing time, decreased participation, raised anxiety, makes the case that wait time isn't a soft nicety but has direct, specific costs when compressed.
His "count the wait time" strategy is deliberately mechanical, silently counting seconds, precisely because action bias operates below conscious awareness and needs an external check.

He frames self-reflection outside of observation as building a trustworthy personal baseline, implicitly acknowledging that a teacher's own sense of how long they waited is unreliable under observation pressure.
quotes: They quickly realised that this wasn’t due to the changes in conditions, but that the act of observing the workers itself encouraged them to adapt their behaviour. This led to the discovery of what we now know as the “Hawthorne Effect”.
However, due to the pressure of being observed, teachers might shorten their Wait Times as a result of Action Bias. Action Bias describes how we feel better when we are doing something.

Decreased student participation – When students are given less time to respond, they can be less likely to engage in discussions or share their thoughts, particularly those who require more time to process information or feel less confident speaking up.

Once you decide how long you want to wait, it may be a good idea to silently count the seconds in your head. This practice can help guard against rushing, ensuring that you’re giving all your students enough time to process the information and respond appropriately.
Try to keep your classroom environment as consistent as possible during observations. This can help reduce any anxiety you might feel and eliminate the need for Action Bias.
